Imagine you need to make a decision — say, choosing which job applicant to hire. You don't just pick randomly. You think: "This person must have at least 2 years of experience. They must communicate well. They must be available on weekdays." Each of those requirements is a rule you are using to judge or evaluate something.

Those rules are criteria.

In the simplest terms: criteria are the standards or conditions you use to judge, evaluate, choose, or decide something.
Singular vs. Plural — The Most Important Thing to Know

This is where most people go wrong, so pay close attention.

"Criteria" is actually the plural form. The singular — meaning just one — is "criterion."

Think of it like this:

  • One rule → criterion
  • Two or more rules → criteria

So if you are judging by one standard, you say:

"The most important criterion is price."

If you are judging by multiple standards, you say:

"The criteria for the job include experience, punctuality, and teamwork."

A very common mistake people make is saying "a criteria" or "this criteria is..." — both are grammatically wrong, because "criteria" is already plural. You would never say "a people" or "this people is." Same logic applies here.

✅ Correct❌ Incorrect
one criterionone criteria
the criteria arethe criteria is
a criteriona criteria

Actually, let me just put it in plain words: always say "one criterion" and "two or more criteria." Never say "a criteria." That's the golden rule.
How It Works in Real Life

Criteria show up everywhere decisions are being made. Here are everyday examples:

Buying an apartment: You might decide based on rent, location, and size. Those three things are your criteria for choosing. If you only cared about one thing — say, location — then location is your single criterion.

Grading a student's essay: A teacher might score it on clarity, grammar, argument strength, and evidence. These four things are the criteria by which the essay is judged.

Choosing a restaurant: You might look for good reviews, a vegetarian menu, and affordable prices. Those are your criteria.

A sports competition: Judges score athletes on technique, speed, and style. Those are the judging criteria.

In every case, notice the pattern: someone needs to make a judgment or selection, and criteria are the specific rules or standards they use to do it.

Criteria can be of two types:

Objective criteria are measurable and clear-cut. There is no room for debate.

"The applicant must have a university degree."
"The product must weigh less than 500 grams."
"The student must score at least 70% to pass."

Either someone meets the criterion or they don't. It's a yes or no.

Subjective criteria involve judgment and personal opinion. Reasonable people can disagree.

"The design must look modern."
"The candidate must have good communication skills."
"The essay must be compelling."

These are still criteria — they're still the standards being used — but they require someone to interpret whether the standard has been met.

Real-world decisions usually involve a mix of both.

You'll often see "criteria" used with a few key verbs. Here's how they work:

Meet the criteria / satisfy the criteria — this means something or someone fulfils all the required standards.

"She meets all the criteria for the scholarship."

Set the criteria / establish the criteria — this means you are deciding what the standards will be.

"The committee sets the criteria before judging the entries."

Based on criteria / according to criteria — this means a decision was made by following the standards.

"Students are ranked based on academic criteria."

Strict criteria / clear criteria / specific criteria — these describe how precise or demanding the standards are.

"The selection process involves very strict criteria."

Criteria are essentially the answer to the question: "What exactly are we judging this by?"

Without criteria, decisions become arbitrary — random, inconsistent, and unfair. With criteria, decisions have a rational basis. That's why criteria matter in law, science, job hiring, academic grading, product design, and almost every domain where evaluation takes place.

When someone says "What are the criteria?", they are really asking: "What rules or standards are we using to decide this?" And when you define the criteria clearly, everyone knows exactly what is expected and how things will be judged.

• Criteria = the standards, rules, or conditions used to judge, evaluate, or decide something
  • It is the plural of criterion (one = criterion; many = criteria)
  • Never say "a criteria" — say "a criterion"
  • Criteria can be objective (measurable) or subjective (a matter of judgment)
  • They appear wherever a decision or evaluation is being made
